one_line.text: Chicago economist and 2017 Nobel laureate who spent a career documenting how real humans differ from textbook rational agents — and then built the policy toolkit that exploits the difference kindly.

biography.text: Born in 1945, Thaler built behavioural economics from inside a hostile discipline: his 'Anomalies' columns catalogued the ways markets and people defied rational-choice theory, his collaborations with Kahneman and Tversky wired psychology into economics, and his mental-accounting and self-control work supplied the field's foundations. Long at the University of Chicago's Booth School — the temple of the rationality he heckled — he won the 2017 Nobel Memorial Prize for his contributions to behavioural economics. Nudge (2008, with Cass Sunstein) took the programme into policy; Misbehaving (2015) told the field's history as memoir.

background.text: His method is the anomaly: find behaviour that standard theory forbids — the cab driver quitting early on rainy days, the pension never joined — document it, and build the better model around it. Nudge is that method inverted into design: if biases are predictable, architecture can compensate.

expertise.text: Behavioural economics' co-founder, with the field's top honours and decades of peer-reviewed foundations; also a practitioner — the Save More Tomorrow pension design is his, deployed at scale.

perspective_and_limits.text: Thaler writes as the genial insurgent: jokes first, models second, always on the side of Humans against Econs. The documented limits attach to the programme more than the man — the nudge label's drift, the paternalism objections, and a 2020s effectiveness literature that contests how much the average nudge actually moves.
